title: Your Analog Solutions are The Problem
author: Patrick Dempsey
summary: Writing against the growing 'slow down, go analog' backlash to AI in higher education, this piece argues that instructors imposing personal worldviews through course requirements — handwriting mandates, forced disconnection, mandatory vulnerability — are overreaching their authority regardless of whether the underlying belief is correct. The author's first argument is that a course exists to serve its stated learning objectives, not as a platform for a professor's philosophy of the good life, using a deliberately absurd Philosophy 101/Linux programming analogy to make the point concrete. The second argument is about power: because students must pass a course to avoid real consequences, an instructor's personal requirements are inherently coercive, not freely chosen — illustrated through escalating parody scenarios where a professor imposes calisthenics, decluttering, or forced LLC investments 'for students' own good.' The third argument takes aim at the 'Dead Poets Society' fantasy of the professor as sage, arguing that expertise in a discipline confers no special authority to direct how another adult should live, relate to technology, or find meaning. The piece concludes that even being correct about what benefits someone does not establish the right to compel it through grading power, and that course requirements must trace back to legitimate, defensible learning objectives rather than an instructor's convictions.
points: Argues a course exists to serve its stated learning objectives, not as a platform for an instructor's personal worldview about AI, technology, or 'the good life.'
Uses a deliberately absurd parody (mandatory calisthenics, forced decluttering, compelled LLC investment) to show how easily 'for your own good' requirements become coercive.
Frames the core issue as one of power: because failing a course has real consequences, students cannot meaningfully consent to an instructor's personal mandates.
Attacks the 'Dead Poets Society' myth of the professor-as-sage as having done higher education 'a huge disservice.'
Insists that being correct about a benefit does not establish the authority to impose it through grading.
quotes: With that out of the way—none of that means you have the right to do what you are doing. Requiring analog approaches. Imposing whatever version of mindfulness, vulnerability, community, disconnection, reflection, or personal development you happen to value.

You can’t just say, “Students will be using AI in their jobs . . . therefore we incorporate AI into all our activities,” just as you can’t just say, “Students need human connection . . . therefore we’re going completely analog.
But if you’re making them handwrite because you believe people need to slow down, reconnect with the earth, or have a more embodied relationship with language, that’s your worldview, not the course.
Students need this course. You are teaching this course. You are the person standing between them and the grade they need. QED.
We have smuggled preferred worldviews into our courses, declared them course-adjacent enough to escape scrutiny, and then used our grading authority to force students to participate in them.

It helped cement the fantasy of the faculty member as John Keating: deeply committed to the discipline, radically unorthodox, and somehow uniquely capable of seeing what students need before they can see it themselves.
Expertise in one of those fields does not confer special authority over how another adult should experience technology, relationships, leisure, community, attention, or the good life.
Being right about what might be good for another person does not give you the authority to impose it through a course they need to pass.
